title: Arrival times of an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate
authors: Pascal Naidon, Lucas Happ, Denis Boiron
abstract: The times of flight of an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate are theoretically investigated in the experimentally unexplored regime corresponding to detection close to the trap of the condensate. In this regime, there is no consensus on how to calculate the distribution of times of arrival onto the detector. For non-interacting particles, distinct theoretical predictions have been made in the past. This work analyses how these predictions are modified for an interacting Bose-Einstein condensate. For this purpose, a time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation is solved analytically and numerically.
summary: This work investigates how repulsive interactions modify the predicted arrival time distributions for an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate. By solving the Gross-Pitaevskii equation and comparing multiple theoretical fluxes, the authors show that while interactions cause quantitative changes from non-interacting atoms, measuring in specific expansion regimes offers a path to experimentally distinguish between competing quantum measurement theories.
main_problem: The primary challenge is determining the theoretically consistent distribution of arrival times for an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) when detected very close to its trapping region.
main_result: Interactions modify theoretical predictions for arrival time distributions, and measuring arrivals in loose expansion directions allows probing regimes where different quantum theories yield distinct, testable results.
method: The authors solve the time-dependent Gross-Pitaevskii equation numerically and analytically to derive various flux formulations (density-like, Kijowski, probability) for comparison.
model_or_system: The system is an atomic BEC governed by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The analysis compares results from non-interacting particles against those including repulsive interactions ($g|\psi|^2$).
key_observables: Arrival-time distribution $\Pi(t)$ onto a detector surface, comparing density flux, Kijowski flux ($\Pi_K$), and probability flux ($F$).
important_parameters: The comparison is highly dependent on the detection separation ($\Delta x$ or $\Delta z$) relative to the initial trap size ($\sigma$), especially in the short-distance regime.
main_assumptions: Approximations include using the scaling Thomas-Fermi method for dynamics and assuming specific forms for quantum flux calculations, though the paper aims to test these limits.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate arrival-time distributions comparing interacting vs. non-interacting cases, showing convergence towards falling flux at large separations but distinct behavior at small separations.
paper_structure: The work systematically reviews multiple theoretical approaches for arrival time measurement, first analyzing the general free-fall case with gravity, then extending these analyses to include mean-field interactions via the GPE and scaling approximations.
why_interesting: This paper tackles a fundamental ambiguity in quantum measurement theory—defining particle detection flux near the source—using the highly controllable platform of BECs to test theoretical boundaries.
